operatorProfile.notesBody: My work often sits at the meeting point of design and implementation. My focus is not the artefacts, but the systems that generate them - interface logic, motion templates, and production pipelines that scale while output remains consistent.

files.title: Summary
files.body: Creative technologist working across product design, media pipelines, and technical prototyping. I lead briefs from specification through to delivery - coordinating external teams, building repeatable frameworks, and shipping across UI, motion, and AI-assisted production.

files.title: Working style
files.body: Structured system design with iterative prototyping. I reduce problems to inputs, constraints, and outputs, then rebuild them as reusable templates rather than one-off solutions - validating design decisions through stakeholder feedback loops until alignment is reached.

files.title: Current focus
files.body: Video generation systems, AI-assisted development pipelines, interface architecture, and tools that reduce the distance between idea and deployed product. Open to permanent creative technologist / AI designer roles and contract engagements - remote, from the UK.

projects.title: Solana Diary
projects.shortDescription: An automated Solana-media pipeline for X: seven services that turned live on-chain data and news into designed, on-brand posts - each one approved by me from Telegram before it published, all running on free-tier APIs.
projects.fullDescription: Solana Diary was an automated media pipeline for X. Seven services on Railway pulled live on-chain data and news and rendered it through a template system I designed - but nothing published until I approved it from Telegram. The pipeline ran on its own code, not on AI: I used AI (Claude, Cursor, Codex) to build it, and Grok was an optional, button-triggered assist for news scoring and copy. I designed the brand and the full set of post templates, and engineered the backend - including the rate-limiting system that kept the whole thing running on free APIs.

projects.role: Solo build - brand, design system & engineering

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Run a Solana-focused media channel on X that publishes designed, on-brand posts every day - both breaking news and on-chain data - without a person doing the daily production, and without ever letting misleading or unsafe information reach the timeline.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: Daily crypto content is a production line: fresh data every few hours, news breaking constantly, and a hard requirement that nothing dangerous goes out. Doing it by hand doesn't scale; fully automating it risks posting bad data or shilling a token that's about to rug. The system had to produce publishable, on-brand work autonomously while keeping me accountable for every single post.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: Seven services on Railway, which I architected and built solo - using AI (Claude, Cursor, Codex) as the build tool, not as part of the running system. An hourly CRON scheduler drove everything: at set times it pulled live market and on-chain data from a set of free-tier public APIs and rendered it, in code, through the post templates I'd designed in Figma - every graphic was populated dynamically from the data, not generated by AI. A rate-limiting layer was central to the whole thing: because it ran entirely on free APIs, I chose providers with per-second rather than monthly limits and paced every request, so it could poll all day and stay current without breaching a quota. Roughly three scheduled data posts went out per day - trending memecoins, new launches, holder-growth leaders, liquidity flows, biggest movers, weekly safety report and more - with event-driven alerts in between: Pool Spotlights, Single-Token Spotlights, and Security Alerts. Grok was an optional, built-in assist I triggered by button - it scored and drafted news stories from a shortlist of channels and suggested copy. Nothing ran end-to-end on its own: every asset and story arrived in Telegram for sign-off, and a set of reply-to commands let me edit fields, rewrite copy, or drop dangerous tokens the APIs had surfaced before anything reached X.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: Nothing ran fully unattended - one misleading post about a rugging token is worse than any amount of manual effort - so approval stayed human. The system did all of the gathering, rendering, and drafting; my decision came down to a tap, or a quick reply-to edit, per post. Two constraints shaped the engineering. Cost: the whole thing ran on free APIs, so the rate-limiter - favouring per-second-limited providers and pacing every call - was what made all-day data possible with no paid plan. Safety: the reply-to layer existed specifically to kill bad data before it hit the timeline - low rugcheck scores, mislabelled fields, unsafe tokens. Even the news automation was deliberately capped: most days it was allowed only a handful of automated calls, though it could technically have fired every second. It shipped with a magazine-style web front end that mirrored every post, but that wasn't rebuilt after a later backend rewrite, so the channel became the product.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Seven cooperating Railway services; a rate-limited data layer over free-tier public APIs; a code-driven rendering engine that populated my Figma templates from live data; a Telegram bot for approvals and reply-to edits; the X API for publishing; and an optional Grok assist for news scoring and copy. On the design side: a template system of roughly fifteen post families on a shared Space Grotesk / IBM Mono type system, a Solana purple-to-green identity, and per-family accent colours (green for momentum, red for risk, purple for news and data) - logo, banner, and every template designed by me.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: It ran daily and did exactly what it was built to do: a designed, on-brand post every few hours, with a human veto on every one. The project ended when X permanently suspended the account for "impersonation" - never specifying the cause, possibly the volume of posted imagery, and declining to reinstate it or explain further. Dead as a product, it's still the most complete system I've shipped solo: seven services, a rate-limited free-API data layer, a code-driven rendering pipeline, a full Telegram approval UX, and a designed template system - proof I can take something from architecture to daily operation on my own, and a sharp lesson that platform risk is a first-class design constraint the moment you automate publishing.

projects.title: UNCX Company Rebrand
projects.shortDescription: Two-phase rebrand: a name and logo overhaul in 2022, then a full brand system and website redesign in 2024 - I wrote the brief and spec, an external team delivered the foundations, and I finished the system in-house.
projects.fullDescription: The UNCX Network rebrand happened in two stages. In 2022 I led a solo rebrand covering the company name change and primary logo. In 2024 an external team worked from my brief and design specification to deliver a full brand system and website redesign in Figma. I then brought the work in-house, completing content, layout, and graphics across 10+ pages.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Evolve the UNCX Network brand across two phases - an initial name and logo change, then a comprehensive brand system and website redesign across the multi-chain DeFi ecosystem.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: The existing brand was inconsistent - different visual treatments per product, no systemised colour or typography logic, and marketing outputs that didn't align with the product UI. The first rebrand addressed the name and mark; the second tackled the full system.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: I wrote the brief and design specification for the 2024 rebrand. An external team delivered the brand system and website redesign in Figma. I then brought the project in-house, completing content, layout refinements, and graphic production across all product pages.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: The first phase in 2022 was driven by a short-notice rebrand requirement, demanding a swift name and identity change with minimal runway. The second phase in 2024 introduced a different constraint: the external team delivered strong initial concepts, colour direction, and brand foundations, but struggled to populate the website designs with accurate product content - they understood the design system but lacked domain knowledge of the products. Hand-holding the content population wasn't sustainable, so I brought the project in-house, completing the website designs, content, and graphics on the foundations they'd set. The final resistance came in implementing the designs consistently across the development subteams.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Delivered brand guidelines, Figma component libraries, website page designs across 10+ product pages, marketing visual templates, and motion style references.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Achieved consistent visual output across all platforms and products. The split approach - external team for brand foundations, in-house for product-specific execution - became the working model. Brand alignment across product teams took longer than the design work itself, but the system now supports coherent output without design drift.

projects.title: UNCX Video & 3D System
projects.shortDescription: End-to-end video production pipeline spanning Cinema 4D, After Effects, and Redshift - built for repeatable, high-frequency output.
projects.fullDescription: A modular production system covering 3D scene assembly in Cinema 4D, Redshift rendering, After Effects compositing, and templated timeline structures. Designed so that product launches, explainers, YouTube tutorials, and partner content could all ship from the same asset library without rebuilding from scratch each time.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: UNCX Network needed a repeatable video system that could support product launches, explainer series, YouTube tutorials, and partner content - without rebuilding from scratch for every deliverable.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: Production was fragmented across freelancers and one-off files. No shared asset library, no consistent motion language, and no templated pipeline - every video started from zero.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: Built a modular pipeline: reusable 3D scenes and camera rigs in Cinema 4D, Redshift lighting presets, templated After Effects compositions with established layout and edit conventions for consistent tone and pacing across formats.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: Time was the primary constraint - I ran the full production pipeline solo alongside other responsibilities. Early videos were over-scoped: lengthy scripts from the marketing team, unique animations per scene, and tight delivery timelines. The key pivots were introducing script length restrictions, stripping back unnecessary scenes, and replacing per-scene custom animation with categorised, reusable templates. The system evolved from complex one-off productions into a streamlined pipeline optimised for volume without sacrificing brand consistency.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Delivered as a production system: Cinema 4D scene templates, After Effects project structures, Redshift material libraries, YouTube thumbnail templates, and established motion conventions baked into the project files.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Cut production time significantly across campaigns. Enabled consistent, brand-aligned output regardless of content type - from 60-second launch trailers to long-form educational content for the Academy. The constraint-driven simplification became the system's strength: fewer unique elements, faster turnaround, more consistent output.

projects.title: UNCX Academy Brand & Platform
projects.shortDescription: Educational platform brand and design system - logotype, component library, article system, video pages, and glossary for DeFi learning.
projects.fullDescription: Brand and platform design for UNCX Academy. I wrote the brief and design specification; an external team delivered the initial design system - custom logotype, component library, and page templates - and I brought the project in-house, completing designs for article categorisation, video learning pages, glossary, integrations hub, and about page, ready for development. My video production system was integrated to produce the platform's educational library.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Design a complete educational platform brand and UI for UNCX Academy - covering identity, page designs, content structure, and a reusable component system.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: DeFi education content was scattered across blog posts, YouTube videos, and documentation with no unified platform, no consistent visual language, and no structured learning progression.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: I wrote the brief and design specification. An external team delivered the logotype, brand identity, and modular Figma component library. I then brought the project in-house, refining content structure across articles, videos, glossary entries, and integrations - each with its own page template and navigation pattern.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: Having navigated similar external-team constraints during the rebrand, I applied a more structured handoff process for the Academy. The external design team delivered strong foundational work - logotype, component library, and page templates - but lacked the product context to complete content-specific designs. I designed the hero graphics, page visuals, and layout specifics, then handed finished designs to an in-house developer who built the site and backend CMS. The video production system integrated seamlessly, as the platform and video content were built from the same brand specification. Beyond launch, I still produce all article header banners for the marketing team's ongoing output.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Complete Figma design system: logotype, component library, page templates for Main, Articles, Videos, Glossary, Integrations, and About. Finished in-house and prepared for development handoff with supporting brand guidelines.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Enabled UNCX Network to launch a structured education platform aligned with the parent brand. The video production system fed directly into the Academy's content library, and my ongoing production of article banners, page graphics, and video content created a single-source creative pipeline across the entire platform.

projects.title: UNCX Unified Menu
projects.shortDescription: Cross-product navigation component system with variable-driven Figma prototypes, research-backed hierarchy, and scalable state logic.
projects.fullDescription: A unified menu system designed to work across UNCX's entire product suite. Built as a variable-driven Figma component with researched navigation patterns, prototype states (open/closed), configurable content slots, and a scalable hierarchy that adapts to different product contexts.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Design a unified navigation component that could work across all UNCX Network products and platforms - replacing inconsistent platform menus with a single scalable system.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: Each UNCX Network product had its own navigation pattern. Users moving between EVM tools, Solana products, Academy, and the homepage encountered different menu structures, creating cognitive overhead and inconsistent UX.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: Researched navigation patterns and hierarchy models. Designed a component-based menu with configurable content slots, variable-driven Figma states, and a scalable hierarchy that adapts per product context.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: The project is on hold due to a shift in development priorities. The core design challenge was fitting multiple products and sub-brands into a single menu structure that remained efficient and navigable. An additional constraint was that the products are highly specialised - the menu needed to be mildly educational, helping users understand what each product does without slowing down experienced users. The main design compromise centred on hierarchy: several products generate significantly more revenue than others and needed visual priority, without devaluing the rest of the ecosystem.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Delivered a Figma design system component with documented states, variables, content slot patterns, and implementation specifications for the development team.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Delivered a complete design system ready for implementation. The hierarchy problem - balancing revenue-generating products against the broader ecosystem - was resolved by establishing definitive levels of hierarchy and de-prioritising non-value generating menu options. Currently on hold pending a shift in development priorities.

projects.title: UNCX App Prototyping
projects.shortDescription: Rapid prototyping across token minting, launchpad flows, Telegram bots, NFT minting, and full launchpad concepts - from wireframes to interactive concepts.
projects.fullDescription: A body of product concepting work spanning multiple UNCX Network features: token minter prototyping, launchpad UI components, Telegram chatbot and presale app flows, NFT minting interfaces, stealth launch concepts, and full launchpad concepts.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Rapidly prototype and validate product concepts across UNCX Network's feature pipeline - covering token minting, launchpad flows, Telegram integrations, and NFT tooling.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: New product features were being scoped without visual validation. Developers were building from text specs, leading to misalignment between design intent and implementation.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: A broad range of product concepts and prototypes spanning different stages and purposes. Some were built and shipped - token minter flows, launchpad components, and Telegram bot interactions. Others remained as design explorations - stealth launch interfaces, NFT minting tools, and full launchpad concepts. Each served to validate direction, align stakeholders, or define scope before committing development resources.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: A recurring constraint across all concepts was incomplete requirements - specifications arrived gradually as projects developed, often requiring rework of existing prototypes. This made component-based design systems essential: rebuilding from reusable parts reduced the cost of iteration. Figma's later introduction of the variables system further reduced component creation overhead. A foundational part of each project was creating FigJam flow diagrams for novel product processes. These weren't problems with established UX conventions to reference - they required working out how the interactions should function from first principles.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Delivered Figma prototypes for each feature area: token minting (blueprint and standard), launchpad components, Telegram bot/app flows, NFT minting interfaces, stealth launch admin, and full launchpad flow diagrams.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Closed the gap between product specs and development handoff. The component-first approach meant that incomplete or shifting requirements - a constant across a five-year span of prototyping - could be absorbed without starting from scratch. Stakeholders could validate features visually before committing development resources, reducing rework and accelerating shipping.

projects.title: Badger Club App
projects.shortDescription: Full-stack badge tracking platform with dark/light themes, role-based dashboards, Supabase backend, and Resend email integration.
projects.fullDescription: A multi-role product system managing badge progress tracking, leader administration, parent communication, and public-facing group pages. Built with React, Supabase, Resend email integration, and Cloudflare security. Supports dark and light themes with a structured database schema designed for scalable group management.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Build a badge tracking system that reduces admin overhead for group leaders while giving parents and children clear visibility into progress and achievements.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: Badge tracking was manual - spreadsheets, paper records, and inconsistent communication between leaders and parents. Leaders carried the full admin burden with no structured tooling.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: Separated the system into operational layers: leader management dashboards for badge administration, parent-facing views for monitoring progress, child-friendly progress visualisation, and public group pages with Cloudflare messaging security.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: Initially envisioned as a multi-user platform with accounts for leaders, parents, and children. Legal and complexity constraints forced a pivot: the app became leader-only, with parent and child interactions designed to work without any account or sign-up. A full inbox and messaging system was also scoped but simplified - mirroring messages across a leader inbox, leader email, and parent email added significant complexity through Resend. The compromise: leaders manage messages via an in-app inbox with email notifications, while parents receive messages directly by email. Development was managed solo using AI-assisted tooling, with phases scoped as atomised tasks to prevent drift during autonomous builds.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Full-stack implementation: React frontend with role-based routing, Supabase backend with structured schema, Google OAuth for authentication, Resend for transactional emails, and Cloudflare for security and performance.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Eliminated manual tracking overhead. The constraint-driven simplification - leader-only accounts, no-signup parent access, streamlined messaging - produced a leaner product with fewer barriers to adoption. Created a scalable foundation with subscription-based monetisation and clear paths for feature expansion.

projects.title: Noticia Lingo App
projects.shortDescription: Language learning app with an AI-assisted classroom, real news articles, Google authentication, Supabase backend, and structured quiz flows.
projects.fullDescription: A language learning platform that transforms live news content into structured learning experiences. Built with React, Supabase, and Google OAuth - featuring article-based lessons, interactive quizzes, a learner dashboard, and a settings system. Designed to replace static flashcard approaches with contextual, real-world content.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Build a language learning system that uses real-world news content instead of static lessons - making vocabulary acquisition contextual and engaging.

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: Traditional language apps rely on decontextualised flashcards and repetitive drills. Learners lose motivation because the content feels disconnected from real usage.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: Content pipeline: ingest news articles, extract vocabulary, generate contextual quizzes, and structure progressive difficulty. User system: Google OAuth, learner profiles, progress tracking, and configurable settings.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: The primary constraint has been lesson complexity. Initial development using AI tooling produced oversimplified quiz questions rather than the pure-function puzzle systems I had specified - lessons that work contextually against any news article, not static question-and-answer pairs. The pivot: expanding the roadmap into granular build phases, constructing each of the 8-10 lesson types step by step with greater complexity control. Technical implementation - Google OAuth, Supabase integration - proved straightforward by comparison. The system is currently focused on Spanish to validate the lesson architecture before introducing multi-language complexity, where each lesson type will need adapting per language.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: Working prototype with React frontend, Supabase backend, Google authentication, structured article reading flow, quiz system, and learner dashboard.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: Demonstrated a scalable learning system driven by live content. The shift from AI-generated simple quizzes to the pure-function lesson types I designed produced a more robust foundation. Active development, with multi-language expansion planned once the core 8-10 lesson types are validated in Spanish.

projects.title: This Site: An Agentic Build System
projects.shortDescription: This portfolio is itself a case study - designed with Figma Make and built by a prompt system that walks a phased roadmap, executing build and QA tasks in an iterative loop.
projects.fullDescription: The site you're reading was produced by a working AI development pipeline: a roadmap decomposed into atomised phases, a custom prompt system that executes each phase with Claude Code and Codex, automated build and QA gates between steps, and human review at phase boundaries. The same approach ships my product work.

overlaySections.title: Brief
overlaySections.body: Rebuild my portfolio - and treat the build itself as the demonstration: how much production software can an AI pipeline ship when the human supplies direction, taste, and review?

overlaySections.title: Problem Frame
overlaySections.body: AI-assisted development fails in two familiar ways: drift, where the agent wanders off-spec during long builds, and mush, where many small edits erode the architecture. Both are process problems, not model problems.

overlaySections.title: System Design
overlaySections.body: A roadmap document decomposes the build into phases, and each phase into atomised tasks with acceptance criteria. A custom prompt system feeds one phase at a time to the coding agent, runs build and QA checks as gates between steps, and stops at phase boundaries for human review. Design direction comes from Figma Make; Claude Code and Codex execute; git history is the audit trail.

overlaySections.title: Trade-offs
overlaySections.body: Atomised tasks cost planning time up front - but they are what prevents drift during autonomous stretches. Phase gates trade raw speed for reviewability: I would rather approve ten coherent checkpoints than untangle one five-thousand-line diff. Where the agent's output disagreed with the spec - and it happens - the roadmap won: the system treats the plan as the source of truth, and plan changes are explicit edits rather than silent divergence.

overlaySections.title: Delivery
overlaySections.body: This site: React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind 4, a JSON content model, a serverless contact relay with rate limiting, and a test suite - shipped through the loop described above.

overlaySections.title: Outcome
overlaySections.body: A production site whose commit history doubles as evidence of the workflow. The same pattern - spec, phased roadmap, gated autonomous execution - is how I now approach product builds: AI provides the throughput, the system provides the discipline, and I provide the judgement.
